summary:
Project Details *
VIGIL is an offline, single-page early-warning dashboard for astronaut fatigue and wellbeing. It combines three tools:

Fatigue index. Short reaction, memory and tracking tasks, modeled on the psychomotor vigilance test used in spaceflight research, are compared with each astronaut’s own baseline. They are combined with sleep, exercise and radiation context into a 0-100 index that flags nominal, early-warning and risk states.
Interactive body map. Nine organs show how microgravity, radiation and isolation can affect them, with a rotating daily exercise routine for each.
Camera check. An on-device camera or photo check estimates posture and joint alignment using pose landmarks, with no data leaving the device.

It addresses the challenge by catching declining performance early, before it becomes an error or a medical event, and by suggesting countermeasures. This matters most on long missions such as Mars, where crews cannot rely on real-time ground support. VIGIL gives screening signals, not diagnoses, and is built on NASA-STD-3001 and Human Research Program material. Next steps are validation with analog-mission data and wearable sensors.
details:
What it does and how it works

VIGIL is a single HTML page that runs offline in any modern browser. It has four parts:

Fatigue index. The astronaut does short reaction-time, working-memory and tracking tasks, which follow the logic of the psychomotor vigilance test used in spaceflight fatigue research. Each result is compared with that person’s own baseline. The index is 95 minus penalties, limited to 0-100. The penalties come from slower responses, more errors, higher variability, sleep below 7.5 h, exercise below 120 min and radiation above 0.5 mSv/day. Above 70 is nominal, 55-70 is early warning and below 55 is risk.

Crew view. Three simulated astronauts are tracked over 30 mission days, with a day slider and a trend chart, to show how the index would work for a whole crew.

Interactive body map. Nine organs (brain, heart, lungs, kidneys, leg muscles, eyes, nose and sinuses, inner ear, throat) each explain the risks outside Earth, what the organ depends on, how it is affected, what an astronaut may feel, how to stay safe and how to recover. Each organ links to a general wellness routine, and a 9-day rotation picks the day’s focus from the device’s local date.

Camera posture check. A front-view photo or live camera frame is analysed by MediaPipe Pose. VIGIL measures shoulder tilt, hip tilt, trunk lean and the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee angles, then compares them with reference ranges. Processing stays on the device.

Benefits and intended impact

It spots declining performance early, before it becomes an error or a medical event.

It works with no connection and no ground-station support, which matters on long missions where communication is delayed.

It uses only a screen and a camera, so there is no extra hardware to carry.

It is meant to support crew self-monitoring and medical-officer decisions, and to help people understand how spaceflight affects their own body.

Tools and technology

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single self-contained file, with inline SVG for the body map and charts.

Google MediaPipe Pose, loaded from a CDN on first use, for body landmark detection.

Browser camera and file-upload APIs.

Reference material from NASA-STD-3001 and the NASA Human Research Program, plus sample radiation and sleep context from NASA OSDR and NOAA space weather data, embedded in the page.

Hardware: any laptop, tablet or phone with a camera.

Creativity

VIGIL links fatigue, the whole body and posture in one tool instead of treating them separately. Each astronaut’s own baseline is the benchmark, not a population average. The camera check needs no wearable, and the rotating organ routines turn the health data into daily actions.

What the team considered

Safety. The page repeatedly says it gives screening signals, not diagnoses, and the exercise text tells users to stop if they feel unwell and to follow the mission medical officer.

Privacy. Camera images are processed on the device.

Data limits. The crew data is simulated and fictional.

Camera limits. Camera angle, clothing and lighting affect the posture measurements.

Offline use. The page is built to open without a connection, but the pose model downloads on first use.
